prompt: A teammate opens an update with: "Over three weeks I pulled the event logs, reconciled them against billing, found duplicate charges, removed them, and re-ran the model." The actual news is that the revenue forecast dropped eight percent. Critique that opening.

criteria: Names that the eight percent drop arrives last instead of first
Says a reader may stop or be interrupted before reaching the news
Proposes a first line that leads with the forecast change
Keeps the reconciliation detail in the message rather than deleting it

prompt: The same finding can go into a memo the reader scrolls at their own pace, or into a live meeting where you may be interrupted at any moment. Where does putting the conclusion first matter more, and for what reason?

options: The meeting, because an interruption can arrive before you ever reach the conclusion
The meeting, because opening with the conclusion shortens the meeting
The memo, because the conclusion needs supporting sections stacked beneath it
Neither, because order changes how it feels but not what is understood

prompt: You have four pieces of a short update and thirty seconds of someone's attention. Put them in the order that survives being cut off halfway through.

items: How the estimate was produced, step by step
The answer: the pipeline can be ready by the 14th
The caveat you would raise only if asked
The two constraints that drive that date

prompt: A director messages you at 4:55pm: "Is the churn number in tomorrow's deck wrong?" It is — a filter dropped trial accounts and overstated churn by about three points. Write the reply you send.

criteria: Opens with the verdict — the number is wrong — in the first sentence
Gives the size or direction of the error before explaining the cause
Puts the filter problem after the answer, not as a preamble to it
Ends with what happens next and when a corrected figure arrives

prompt: The result of a pipeline migration has to go to the engineer who will maintain it and to the executive who funded it. Explain what you change between the two versions and what stays identical.

criteria: Names something the engineer already knows that the executive does not
States what each of the two will do with the information
Keeps the underlying finding and numbers the same in both versions
Names the executive's real worry — cost, risk, or timing — rather than assuming interest in mechanics

prompt: Match each reader of the same pipeline write-up to the thing they are actually worried about.

left: A finance partner reviewing your forecast
The on-call engineer inheriting the pipeline
A support lead whose team fields the complaints
An executive deciding whether to fund another quarter
right: What pages them at 3am, and how to make it stop
Whether the last quarter of spend produced anything
How many customers notice, and what to tell them
Whether the range is defensible enough to put in a budget

prompt: Before writing up a result, which questions actually tell you how to pitch it?

options: What will this person do with the answer once they have it?
What do they already know, so I am not re-explaining it?
What are they afraid is going wrong?
Which part of the work was the hardest to build?
Which chart style will look best on the slide?

prompt: Adjusting a message to its audience can slide into telling people what they want to hear. Where is the line, and how do you know when you have crossed it?

criteria: Separates changing the framing from changing the conclusion
Gives a case where an unwelcome finding has to survive the translation
Names what stays fixed no matter who is in the room
Offers a check for whether the message has been softened past the evidence

prompt: A weekly load that feeds the leadership dashboard silently dropped one of its sources last Tuesday. You discover it on Friday afternoon and decide to raise it at Monday's standup instead. What breaks first over that weekend, and who pays for the delay?

criteria: Names a decision someone makes on the stale numbers before Monday
States that the cost of the slip grows with every day it is unreported
Identifies the risk that someone else finds it and reports it first
Says what could still be salvaged by speaking on the Friday

prompt: Put these steps in the order you would take them on the day you realise a committed deadline is going to be missed.

items: Send the agreed plan in writing to everyone downstream
Tell the owner the date has moved and walk them through the options
Notice the task is behind and confirm how many days are at stake
Draft two recovery options and price each one in scope and time

prompt: True or false: sitting on a known two-week slip until you have a confirmed recovery plan spares the stakeholder unnecessary noise. Say why.

criteria: Says the stakeholder loses days they could have spent re-planning
Names the trust cost when they hear about it from someone else
States that options can be offered before a plan is confirmed
Separates a rough date with a caveat from giving no signal at all
Says the stakeholder loses days they could have spent re-planning
Names the trust cost when they hear about it from someone else
States that options can be offered before a plan is confirmed
Separates a rough date with a caveat from giving no signal at all

prompt: It is Wednesday afternoon and you have just worked out that a migration promised for the end of the month will land about two weeks late. Write the short message you send to the sponsor today.

criteria: Leads with the date moving rather than with the explanation
Gives a revised date, or a date by which a firm date will exist
Offers at least two options the sponsor can choose between
Stays under five sentences with no apology preamble

prompt: A fix you shipped changes a metric definition that three other teams quote in their own reporting. Beyond replying to the person who reported it, what does closing the loop require?

options: Nothing further — the person who reported it can pass the word along
Telling the teams who quote that metric what changed and from which date
Rebuilding every historical report yourself before saying anything to anyone
Waiting for someone to notice the discrepancy and then explaining the change

prompt: A colleague tells you that announcing your own finished work is self-promotion, and that the work should speak for itself. Argue against that.

criteria: Names who is left without information when nothing is announced
Points out that nobody outside the work can see that it finished
Separates reporting an outcome from claiming credit for it
Describes a low-cost form the announcement can take

prompt: True or false: if the person who requested a change has not chased it in a month, the change stopped mattering to them, so there is no need to tell them it shipped.

criteria: Says silence usually means they routed around the gap instead
Notes they may still be running a workaround built on the old behaviour
States the cost of sending the note as near zero either way
Points out the requester has no way to learn it shipped unless told
Says silence usually means they routed around the gap instead

prompt: Six weeks ago someone reported that a report double-counted refunds. The fix went live this morning and nobody has asked about it since. Write the note you send them.

criteria: States in the first line that the fix is live
Says what the numbers show now that they did not before
Tells them whether figures they saved earlier have changed
Gives one concrete thing to look at or a way to reply

prompt: Someone is asked how many active users the product has and replies: "It depends what you mean by active, the event data has gaps in April, and the mobile SDK undercounts, so I'd rather not give a number until I've dug in." Critique that reply.

criteria: Points out that the reply contains no figure at all
Says caveats belong after a number, not in place of one
Rewrites it as a figure with a range and a stated definition
Keeps only the caveat that would change what the asker does

prompt: A product manager asks how much revenue a weekend checkout bug cost. You have order counts for the affected hours but no record of the sessions that failed. Give the answer you would say out loud, with the number and how sure you are of it.

criteria: Gives a low and a high figure rather than one number
Attaches a stated confidence or likelihood to that range
Names the single unknown that drives most of the spread
Says what would narrow the range and how long that would take

prompt: You are about 80 percent sure that a data-quality problem touches between 2 and 5 percent of rows, and a director asks you how big it is. Which reply gives them the most to act on?

options: Somewhere between 2 and 5 percent of rows, and I'd be surprised if it fell outside that
Roughly 3.4 percent of rows
I can't say anything until the audit finishes next week
Hard to know — there are several known issues with that data

prompt: Which of these turn a rough estimate into something a decision-maker can actually use? Select all that apply.

options: Stating an explicit low and high figure
Saying how confident you are that the truth sits in that range
Listing every assumption you made before you state the number
Naming the one input that would move the number most
Rounding to a precision that matches what you actually know
Quoting the figure to two decimal places to show the work was careful

prompt: Complete the sentence that turns a scope problem into someone else's decision rather than your private slip: "Here's what I'd ___, and here's what that ___ you."
Match each squeeze to the move that fits it.

left: The deadline is fixed by an outside commitment
The full list matters more than the launch date
One item waits on a source that arrives next month
Every item is required and the date cannot move
right: Hold the list and move the date
Split into two phases with that item in the second
Ask for another person, or knowingly drop a quality step
Cut the lowest-value items and say which ones went

prompt: Your lead says: "Keep all six dashboards in the first release — we can't drop any of them." Two of the six depend on a data source that will not exist for another month. Write your reply.

criteria: Names which specific items you would move out of the release
States what the lead gives up if those items are cut
Prices the alternative — a later date, or more people on it
Ends by asking for a decision rather than registering a complaint

prompt: When is proposing a scope cut the wrong response to a schedule squeeze, and what do you put on the table instead?

criteria: Names a case where the item at risk is the point of the project
Says the tradeoff belongs to whoever owns the outcome, not to you
Gives an alternative such as re-sequencing or asking for help
States that a silent slip or a weekend push is still not the answer

prompt: A ticket carries this as its finish line: "Done when the numbers look right and the requester is happy with it." Pull that apart and give a version you would agree to.

criteria: Points out that looks right names no check against anything
States that satisfaction has no end point, so revisions never stop
Adds a figure or source the output must reconcile against
Names a single person who does the accepting

prompt: Someone asks you for "a dashboard for churn". Explain what you would pin down before writing any code, and name the later argument each one heads off.

criteria: Names the artifact that will exist at the end in concrete terms

Names a condition that would make the output wrong
Ties at least one item to a revision cycle it prevents

prompt: Which of these belong in a finish line agreed with the requester before any work starts? Select all that apply.

options: The exact artifact that will exist when the work stops
The named person who checks it and accepts it
A known figure the output has to reconcile against
The list of every function and query you plan to write
The condition under which the result would be wrong
The tool or language you intend to build it in

prompt: You have been handed a vague request. Order these four moves as you would make them in the kickoff conversation.

items: Restate the whole thing back and get a yes in writing
Name the single person who will accept the result
Ask what decision the output is going to feed
Agree the figure or check the output must match

prompt: A hiring manager who has heard a lot of overclaiming asks what your reliability work achieved. Which phrasing survives their scepticism?

options: I dramatically improved the reliability of our reporting
Failed runs went from about four a month to zero, and stayed there for a quarter
I owned the reporting reliability workstream

prompt: A manager drafting your review writes "cut report runtime by 90%". The real figure was 35 percent, and a colleague did the indexing that produced most of it. Write what you say to them.

criteria: Corrects the number to the one you can defend if challenged
Names the colleague's contribution rather than absorbing it
Keeps the part of the claim that is yours instead of waving it all off
Says why the accurate figure is still worth putting in the review

prompt: One line of this account of a past project undermines the rest of it. Which line, and why?

lines: Our weekly finance report took six hours and failed overnight most weeks.
I profiled the job and found one join scanning the full history every run.
I rewrote it to read only the partitions that had changed.
Single-handedly, I saved the company millions of dollars a year.
Runtime went from six hours to twenty minutes and it has not failed since.
answer.why: It swaps a measurable result for an unverifiable claim and takes sole credit for it. The runtime figure on the next line is the part a listener can check, and the inflated line makes them doubt it.

prompt: An interviewer asks what you did on your last project, a pipeline rewrite. Give the answer in under ninety words: the situation, what you did, and what came of it.

criteria: Opens with the situation and what was wrong with it
States what you personally did, separate from what the team did
Closes on a result carrying a specific measured number
Claims no credit for the parts other people delivered

prompt: You circulate a document that opens with the proposed table layout and never states what is wrong today. What breaks first once people start commenting?

criteria: Says reviewers argue over details instead of over the goal

criteria: States that a reader cannot disagree without knowing the alternatives

Names the cost of re-arguing the same option months later

prompt: Match each section of a design document to the question a reader opens it to answer.

Decision
Consequences
right: Which one we picked, and on what grounds

What is broken today, and for whom
What else we could have done, and why we did not

prompt: True or false: the downsides of the chosen approach are best left out of a design document, since naming them invites readers to reject the proposal. Say why.

criteria: States that reviewers find the unnamed downsides anyway
Says naming the consequences is what makes the document reviewable
Notes the credibility cost when a hidden cost surfaces after the fact
Separates stating a cost from arguing against the choice
States that reviewers find the unnamed downsides anyway
Says naming the consequences is what makes the document reviewable
Notes the credibility cost when a hidden cost surfaces after the fact

Names that the first real reaction arrives after the cost is already sunk

prompt: A stakeholder cannot say what they want from a new report, and you have one afternoon before you speak to them again. Which of these is most likely to surface a disagreement about what they actually want?

options: A written list of clarifying questions sent ahead of the meeting
A rough one-page mock with invented numbers, laid out the way you think they meant
A summary of what teams in similar roles usually track

prompt: True or false: building a mock on invented numbers wastes the afternoon, because nobody can judge the output until it is wired to real data. Say why.

criteria: States that layout, grain and choice of measure can be judged before the data is real

criteria: States that the numbers in the mock are made up and must not be quoted

prompt: Fill in the two blanks: an estimate that survives being repeated second-hand gives a ___ instead of a single date, and names the ___ that would push the work past the top end of it.
Asked for a delivery date, an engineer answers: "Two weeks, assuming nothing surprising." Critique that as an estimate the asker is about to repeat to their own boss.

criteria: Points out it will be passed on as the single date two weeks
Says that assuming nothing surprising names no actual risk
Supplies a rewrite carrying a lower and an upper bound

prompt: You are asked on the spot how long it takes to add three new fields to an existing nightly load. You have never touched the upstream system those fields come from. Give the answer you would say out loud.

criteria: Gives two numbers as a range rather than one date
Names the specific thing that would push it past the top of the range

prompt: You have said a piece of work will take two to four weeks. Which of these make it harder for that to get repeated as "two weeks"?

options: Naming the specific thing that would make it four rather than two

Adding "give or take" without saying give or take what

prompt: Someone in legal asks why a dashboard they opened this morning disagrees with the screenshot they took yesterday, when nobody touched it. prompt: Match each thing you might say at the end of an explanation to what it actually gets you.

left: "Does that make sense?"
"If your director asks you this tomorrow, what would you tell them?"
"I can go deeper on the mechanics, or stop here — which is more useful?"
"Sorry, this part is quite technical."
right: Their own version of it, which shows you what survived
A hint that you expect them not to follow, which is what they hear
A nod that costs nothing and hides whatever is still missing
A read on how much detail they wanted in the first place

prompt: One line of this explanation to a non-technical manager undoes the other four. Which line, and why?

lines: The report was empty this morning because the file we load from never showed up.

In numbers: the 6am load found zero rows for yesterday, so the page had nothing to draw.
The root cause is that the upstream CDC stream lagged past the watermark and the partition got pruned.
It is back now, and tomorrow I can show you the one place to look to see whether the file landed.
answer.why: Every other line stays in words the manager already owns. This one is the sentence that is supposed to deliver the cause, and it spends three terms the listener cannot query without admitting they are lost — so the explanation fails exactly where it matters.

prompt: Reaching for an analogy is the standard move when explaining something technical. When is it the wrong move, and what do you reach for instead?
